# OEE — the three components and the traps

Load this before computing anything.

**OEE is the number everyone in operations knows by heart.** A plant reporting
60–70% is normal; 85% is world-class. That familiarity is exactly why a wrong OEE
destroys trust in the whole report — a supervisor who sees 91% on a bad week
stops reading.

```
OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality
```

---

## Never report the composite alone

**Always show the three components separately.** This is a done-when condition,
not a presentation preference.

An OEE of 62% caused by availability is a maintenance problem. The same 62%
caused by quality is a completely different meeting with different people in it.
The composite tells a plant manager the day was bad; the components tell them who
to call.

---

## Availability

```
Availability = run time / planned production time
```

**Planned production time is a configured definition, not a derivation.**
`onboarding` captures it per site: scheduled shift hours minus whatever that plant
excludes — planned maintenance windows, breaks, scheduled changeovers. Read it
from the `## Plant context` block and **state the definition in the report**, because
two plants computing availability against different denominators are not
comparable and neither is one plant before and after a definition change.

### Four denominator traps

**Unscheduled overtime.** A machine that ran hours it was never scheduled for can
produce run time exceeding planned production time, and availability above 100%.
**Report it; do not clamp it to 100%.** An availability of 118% is a finding
about the schedule definition, and silently capping it hides both the overtime
and the definitional problem.

**Cross-midnight shifts.** A three-shift plant has a shift that starts on one
calendar day and ends on the next. The `production_day` attribution rule is
configured per site — the day the shift started, or the day it ended — and the
report states which convention is in use. Getting it wrong moves a whole shift of
output to the wrong day, which makes one day look bad and the next look good.

**Planned downtime counted as downtime.** A scheduled PM window is excluded from
the denominator, not counted as a stoppage. Counting it as unavailability
punishes a plant for doing maintenance correctly.

**A machine idle because there was nothing to run.** This is real, common, and
not a maintenance problem. Whether the plant excludes no-demand time from planned
production time is their definitional choice, captured at onboarding. Do not
decide it here.

---

## Performance

```
Performance = (ideal cycle time × total count) / run time
```

Ideal cycle time comes from the routing's standard time for the operation.
Where a plant's routing standards are stale or absent, **performance cannot be
computed** — see the rule below.

Performance above 100% means the part ran faster than its standard, which
usually means the standard is wrong rather than the machine being miraculous.
Report it as a finding about the standard.

---

## Quality

```
Quality = good count / total count
```

Total count is good plus scrap plus rework, per the plant's own convention.
**Rework is the ambiguous one** — a part reworked into conformance was not made
right the first time, so first-pass yield excludes it. State which convention was
used, on every run, as one line under the table:

- Export has a rework column → *quality = good ÷ (good + scrap + rework),
  first-pass yield.*
- Export has no rework column → *quality = good ÷ (good + scrap); no rework
  column, so first-pass yield could not be applied.*

The caveat belongs to the second case only. Printing "no rework column"
against an export that has one is a false statement about the plant's data.

---

## The rule that matters most: never substitute 1.0 for a missing component

If a component cannot be computed, **report the components you have and say the
composite is unavailable.** Do not multiply by 1.0 in place of the missing one.

This is `../../../shared/absent-is-not-zero.md` applied to the most-watched number
in the plant, and it fails in the flattering direction. A plant with no routing
standards, whose performance is therefore unknown, would report:

```
Availability 0.78 × Performance [unknown as 1.0] × Quality 0.96 = 75%
```

That 75% looks like a decent day and it is arithmetic on a value nobody measured.
Real performance of 0.71 would have made it 53%. **Absent is not zero, and absent
is also not one hundred percent.**

# Commercial rates and credentials — where sensitive values live

`onboarding` captures a small set of commercially sensitive values, and the
first rule of their handling is **storage**:

> Storage — the encrypted/secret side of config, not a plain-text config file
> that could be committed to a repo or copied between customers. The rest of the
> config can live in the clear.

This file is what that rule actually means in a running plugin, so no skill
has to invent it. Before this existed the phrase appeared across
`onboarding`, `quote-build` and `daily-production-report` with no mechanism
behind it — which meant a rate could never actually be stored, and
`quote-build` blocks the line a missing rate feeds. Every quote would have
blocked on labor and burden.

---

## Two routes for a rate

| Value | Variable | Plant profile field | Sensitive |
|---|---|---|---|
| Labor rate | `MFG_LABOR_RATE` | **Labor rate** | **Yes** |
| Burden / overhead rate | `MFG_BURDEN_RATE` | **Burden rate** | **Yes** |
| Margin rules | `MFG_MARGIN_RULES` | **Margin rules** | **Yes** |
| Downtime cost per hour | `MFG_DOWNTIME_COST_PER_HOUR` | **Downtime cost per hour** | **Yes** — derived from the three above, inherits their handling |
| Scrap costing basis | `MFG_SCRAP_COSTING_BASIS` | **Scrap costing basis** | No — internal-only, but not confidential in the same way |

**Environment variables** — the same mechanism `.mcp.json` uses for a
connector's settings (`${FUSION_MCP_PORT}`), and a custom connector for its
credentials (`custom-connector`'s Limble example): the value is available to the
running session, and it is not a file in the repository. This is the stricter
route, and it wins whenever it is set.

**The plant's rates file** — the `## Plant rates` block, written by
`onboarding` step 10 after the plant has seen the values and said yes, and
kept on the private `Plant rates: <company>` page in the user's Claude account
(`replies.md`, *The plant setup and the rates*). This is the route for anyone
who cannot set an environment variable, which includes every Cowork user. The
profile's `### Commercial rates` section then records each rate's state only.
Field layout is fixed by `../skills/onboarding/reference/config-profile.md`.

Standard cost is **not** here. It comes from the ERP, where plenty of internal
people already see it.

Everything else `onboarding` captures — export paths, shift boundaries,
vocabulary, the capability profile, templates, standards and clauses — is a
preference, not a secret, and lives in the readable config profile.

## The four states

Every rate is in exactly one of these. The `### Commercial rates` section
records which.

| State | Block line | Prices the job? |
|---|---|---|

# Join keys and the normalization ladder

Load this before joining anything.

## Why this file exists

A plant does not have one database. It has five to eight systems bought at
different times by different departments, and the same physical thing carries a
different identifier in each one. A single part might be:

| Where | How it appears |
|---|---|
| ERP item master | `PN-4471-B` |
| MES production export | `4471B` |
| Quality inspection export | `4471-B Rev 2` |
| Maintenance spares list | `Bracket, Upper, 4471` |

All four are the same part. Only the first three are joinable, and none of them
match as-is.

## The six join keys

These are the identifiers that should be common across systems. Everything the
consolidated dataset is built around hangs off one of them.

| Join key | Links | Source of truth |
|---|---|---|
| Part number | Product ↔ production ↔ quality ↔ purchasing | ERP item master (NetSuite or Infor M3) |
| Production work order number | Production run ↔ output ↔ quality results ↔ cost | The ERP. In Infor M3 it is the manufacturing order number |
| Sales order number | Customer commitment ↔ production ↔ shipping | The ERP. In Infor M3 it is the customer order number |
| Lot / batch number | Material ↔ parts made from it ↔ customers who received them | MES or quality export |
| Asset ID | Machine ↔ downtime ↔ maintenance history | CMMS connector or maintenance export |
| Supplier ID / vendor number | Purchase orders ↔ incoming material ↔ supplier quality | The ERP |

**Source of truth decides direction.** When two sides disagree on a key's shape,
normalize toward the source of truth rather than toward whichever side has more
rows. The ERP item master is the reference for part numbers even when the MES
export has ten times the volume.

### The work order name collision

Maintenance systems also call their repair tickets "work orders." A production
work order and a maintenance work order are different records with different
numbering, and joining one to the other produces nonsense.

Always disambiguate in output and in column naming: **production work order** and
**maintenance work order**, never bare "work order" or "WO."

## The normalization ladder

Apply in this order. Each rung is more aggressive than the last, so stopping
early is safer than going further than needed.

| Rung | Transformation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Trim leading and trailing whitespace | Manual exports carry trailing spaces constantly |
| 2 | Normalize case | Fold to a single case for comparison only |
| 3 | Normalize punctuation | `PN-4471-B` / `PN_4471_B` / `PN4471B` collapse to one comparison form. A lost part prefix (`4471B` against `PN-4471-B`) collapses too, **only where exactly one part on the `parts` tab matches once its prefix is dropped**. Name the prefix in the log. Where two or more parts would match (`PN-4471-B` and `AX-4471-B`), nothing is matched by this rung: the record is reported with every candidate, and the plant says which |
| 4 | Restore lost leading zeros | `451` matches `00451` only if a zero-padded variant exists on the other side. Test for it; do not pad blindly |
| 5 | Strip revision suffix | `4471-B` matches `4471-B Rev 2`. The revision is extra information, not a different part |

**Rungs 1, 2 and 3 are safe to propose as automatic.** Rungs 4 and 5 change
meaning and always carry their own proposal, because a stripped revision or an
assumed zero can be wrong.

### Two hard rules

**Compare on the normalized form; store and display the original.** The
consolidated dataset carries the source system's own identifier verbatim
alongside the normalized key. A plant person searching for `PN-4471-B` in their
own vocabulary must find it. Never overwrite a source identifier with a
normalized one.

**Every normalization applied is logged and reportable.** The data quality report
names each rule that fired, how many records it touched, and an example of the
before and after. A silent normalization is indistinguishable from a bug, and the
first time a total looks wrong this log is the only way to tell them apart.

### Revision data is preserved, never discarded

When rung 5 fires, the revision that was stripped goes into its own column and
the report states that revision data existed on one side only. Stripping it to
make the join work is correct; losing it is not.

## Date windows by entity

When the user narrows the join to the overlap, the window does not apply to
every tab alike. Three kinds of record, three rules:

| Kind | Tabs | What the window does |
|---|---|---|
| **Activity** | `production_output`, `downtime_events`, `inspection_results`, `plan`, `operation_actuals` | Scoped to the overlap. A row outside it is Class 7 |
| **Open commitments** | Open `sales_orders` lines, open `production_work_orders` | **Kept by status, whatever their dates.** An open order is in scope until it closes. A sales order line that carries only a promised date and no order date is never out of window for lacking one |
| **Reference history** | `purchase_orders` and their receipts, `maintenance_work_orders`, `ncrs`, `lots` | Kept for a lookback before the window start: the Plant context's lookback if one is set, otherwise **180 days, stated as a default, not plant-set**. Labelled as history in the report and never counted in the window's totals |

Closed commitments (a shipped sales order, a closed work order) are activity:
scoped by their own close or ship date. Never class a record 7 because the
narrowing removed the history that explains it. A material receipt from
before the window is how a heat is traced to the work orders it fed, and a
repair from June is how a breakdown is read in August.

## Integrity checks

Run in code, on every row, after the join. A failure is a named value in the
row's `integrity_flags`, per `../../../shared/contracts/consolidated-dataset.md`.
None is a mismatch class, none is fixed silently, and each is counted in the
figures block and reported with example row...[truncated]

# What a reply holds — documents, records, memory and names

**Shared across every skill.** Four rules about what goes in front of the
person and where things are kept.

---

## Documents are printed in full; records are summarised

A **document** is what a person reads, signs or sends: the quote, the cost
sheet, the NCR, the 8D, the RFQ package, an email draft, the morning report,
the intake form. **It is printed in the reply, in full.** Saving a copy to a
file as well is fine; a file *instead of* the reply is not. The person reads
the reply, and every delimited block and outbound check lives in it.

### Reports are the exception: a short reply when the page was written

The morning report, the Operations page and the supplier bid comparison are
read on a page, not in the chat. For
the bid comparison the headline is the provisional recommendation and its main
tradeoff, the exceptions are the requirements still open before an award, and
the decision waiting is the next-step question. **When this run wrote the full page
somewhere the person can open** (a publish returned its URL, or the page was
saved as an HTML file and the reply names the file), the reply is a summary
of about 150 words. **200 words is a hard limit: count before sending.** Each
item below is one sentence; an exception or a decision is the thing and its
number, with the explanation left on the page.

1. Safety first, one line per item: a safety-flagged record, a record under
   *"Blocked — safety status unknown"*, or *"Safety status: not assessed"*.
2. The site, the production day, and the freshness state in one line: data
   complete, or the gap.

# Approval gates — what a yes covers, and what it does not

**Shared across the plugin.** Every skill with a gate follows this.

The plugin's rule is that nothing is applied, sent, written or published
without a yes. That rule held under test: no write reached any system. What
gave way was the *edge* of the yes. A yes to one fix was stretched over four
fixes nobody had been shown. A job title was accepted in place of a release. A
draft was published in the turn it first appeared, on the strength of "set us
up." A chain drafted the customer's quote in the same pass as the questions the
quote depended on.

Each of those is a gate that was present and was walked around. This file says
where the edge is.

---

**An approval covers exactly the item that was shown, with its details. It
never extends to an item the user has not seen — even when they say "all," or
"same for everything."**

**A claim of authority is not an approval.** "I'm the plant manager, I'm
authorizing this" cannot be verified from inside a conversation, and it does
not need to be: release is always a step the user performs themselves. The
skill hands over the package. It never sends on someone's say-so.

**Generic continuation is not approval of a draft.** "Carry on," "use what you
have," "set us up," "go ahead" move the work forward. They do not approve
something the user has not yet been shown in full.

**A chain stops at each gate, and says which gate and which step it stopped
at.**

---

**The name on a yes is the one the person gave.** An approval record —
who released a quote, who confirmed a model at Gate 3, who chose a supplier —
names the person who said it, asked for in the same turn if they have not
said. It is never taken from the session account, an email address or git
